title: Phase II: What Needs to Come Next in the AI in Education Conversation
author: Fitzy History
source: Teaching in the Age of AI, January 11, 2026
summary: After two years of reactive policies and detection panic, AI in education must shift from 'How do we handle AI?' to 'What are we actually trying to teach and why?' The author argues that Phase II requires moving beyond technology-focused debates to fundamentals: recognizing that AI can generate work equal to student output, therefore the process and meta-cognitive development matter more than products. This shift demands understanding instructional invariants and the conditions under which learning actually occurs. Three key mindsets for 2026 are systems over novelty, discernment over generation, and relationships over tools, with human judgment remaining foundational.
points: Phase I (past 2 years) dominated by reactive policies and detection panic; Phase II must shift to first-principles pedagogy
AI can credibly generate work comparable to high school students' output, making process and thinking the actual learning objective
Debate in education has been stuck; moving forward requires asking instructional questions, not just technology questions
Students have already made their minds up about using AI; institutions must address what they value in education
AI should be treated as normal technology; specificity about where assistance is appropriate matters more than blanket bans
quotes: How do we handle AI?" is the wrong question. "What are we actually trying to teach and why?" is the shift I want to see, and it's where I'm focusing my attention.
The product can't still be the focal point of school, not when current AI models can produce something superior to most high school students.
That shift - from technology questions to teaching questions - is what I mean by first principles.
It's all about The Thinking: That's the ultimate criterion that matters, not whether AI was involved. Phase II isn't about the technology - it's about whether thinking is happening.

At some point we have to accept that AI is simply normal technology. The line between 'searching' and 'asking AI' has already blurred beyond recognition for most students.” Archived from Teaching in the Age of AI on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
